name: -thing ADJ
title: Adjectives after -thing/-body/-one words
description: Compounds like something, nothing, anyone and everybody place the describing adjective right after them, not before, e.g. 'something interesting'.
example: Let's do something fun this weekend.

name: ADVERBS OF ATTITUDES: apparently/clearly/fortunately/frankly/unfortunately
title: Attitude Adverbs (apparently, clearly, fortunately...)
description: Sentence adverbs such as apparently, clearly, fortunately, frankly and unfortunately, usually placed at the start, show the speaker's opinion about the whole sentence.
example: Unfortunately, the train was cancelled.

name: COMPARATIVE OF SUPERIORITY: more+ADJ/ADV
title: Comparatives with more (more + adjective/adverb)
description: Longer adjectives and adverbs form the comparative with more before them instead of an -er ending.
example: This job is more interesting than my last one.

name: COMPARATIVE and COMPARATIVE (the same adjective)
title: Repeated Comparatives (bigger and bigger)
description: Repeating the same comparative form joined by 'and' shows that a quality is continuously increasing or decreasing over time.
example: The traffic in this city is getting worse and worse.

name: COMPARISON OF EQUALITY: not as/so ... as
title: Comparison of Equality: not as/so ... as
description: The pattern 'not as/so + adjective + as' compares two things that are not equal in a certain quality.
example: This film isn't as good as the book.

name: DETERMINER: another
title: Another (determiner and pronoun)
description: Another means 'one more' or 'a different one'; it goes before a singular noun or stands alone as a pronoun.
example: Can I have another coffee, please?

name: INDEFINITE PRONOUN/PROP-WORDS: ones (except for 'one')
title: Ones (as a substitute pronoun)
description: Ones replaces a plural noun already mentioned, so you don't have to repeat it, often after an adjective.
example: I don't like these shoes; I prefer the red ones.

name: INTENSIFIED COMPARATIVES: a lot/by far/even/far/much/still
title: Intensifiers with Comparatives (much, far, even, still)
description: Words like much, far, a lot, even and still are placed before a comparative adjective or adverb to strengthen the degree of difference.
example: This phone is much better than my old one.

name: PASSIVE: PAST
title: Past Passive (was/were done)
description: Formed with was/were + past participle, it focuses on the action or the receiver of the action rather than who did it.
example: The window was broken last night.

name: PHRASAL VERBS (V+NP+PARTICLE)
title: Phrasal verbs (separable: verb + object + particle)
description: Many two-part verbs (like turn off, pick up) can have the object placed between the verb and the particle.
example: Can you turn the lights off, please?

name: POSSESSIVE PRONOUNS (except for 'his' and 'its')
title: Possessive Pronouns (mine, yours, hers, ours, theirs)
description: Possessive pronouns stand in for a possessive noun phrase to show ownership, e.g. 'this seat is mine' instead of 'my seat'.
example: Is this jacket yours or hers?
note: A2-level pronoun set typically mastered before B1; not worth a dedicated lesson at this level.

name: PRONOUN: others (excluding 'the
title: Pronoun: others (without 'the')
description: 'Others' without 'the' means 'other people or things in general', contrasted with something already mentioned, rather than a specific known group.
example: Some people like tea, others prefer coffee.

name: Please+INFINITIVE
title: Please + base verb (polite request)
description: Please is added before an imperative verb to make a request sound more polite, usually at the start of a sentence.
example: Please close the door.

name: RECIPROCAL PRONOUN: each other
title: Reciprocal Pronoun: each other
description: 'Each other' (like 'one another') shows that two or more people direct the same action toward one another, expressing a mutual relationship.
example: We always help each other with our homework.

name: REFLEXIVE PRONOUNS
title: Reflexive Pronouns (myself, yourself, himself...)
description: Reflexive pronouns show the subject and object of a verb are the same person, and are also used to add emphasis to a noun or pronoun.
example: I taught myself how to cook.

name: SUPERLATIVE OF SUPERIORITY: most+ADJ/ADV
title: Superlatives with most (most + adjective/adverb)
description: Longer adjectives and adverbs form the superlative with the most before them instead of an -est ending.
example: That was the most beautiful sunset I've seen.

name: TENSE/ASPECT: FUTURE
title: Future (will / going to / future progressive)
description: Will and be going to express future plans, predictions, and decisions; will/be + -ing (future progressive) describes an action that will be in progress at a future time.
example: I'll call you tonight, and I'm going to visit her tomorrow.

name: TENSE/ASPECT: FUTURE PROGRESSIVE
title: Future Progressive (will be doing)
description: Form the future progressive with 'will be' plus the -ing form to describe an action that will be in progress at a specific future time.
example: Will you be using the car tomorrow morning?

name: TENSE/ASPECT: PAST PERFECT
title: Past Perfect (had done)
description: Form the past perfect with 'had' plus a past participle to show an action completed before another point in the past; 'had been doing' adds emphasis on duration.
example: She had already left when I arrived.

name: TENSE/ASPECT: PAST PROGRESSIVE
title: Past Progressive (was/were doing)
description: Formed with was/were + -ing, it describes an action in progress at a specific past moment, often interrupted by another event.
example: I was watching TV when you called.

name: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT PERFECT
title: Present Perfect (have done)
description: Formed with have/has + past participle, it links the past to now, for finished actions with present relevance, experiences, or ongoing situations (including have been doing).
example: I've lived in this city for five years.

name: These/Those N
title: Demonstratives: these/those + noun
description: 'These' and 'those' are used before plural nouns to point to things that are near or far from the speaker.
example: Those shoes look really comfortable.
note: Elementary A1/A2 demonstrative pattern already familiar before B1; extraction limited by corpus position rules.

name: This/That N
title: Demonstratives: this / that + noun
description: This and that combine with a singular noun to point to something near (this) or far away (that) from the speaker.
example: This book is really interesting.
note: Basic A1-level demonstrative + noun pattern; the sentence-initial restriction is a corpus extraction artefact, not a real teaching point.

name: VERB OBJECT V-ING
title: Verb + object + -ing (see someone doing)
description: Some verbs (like see, hear, watch, keep) are followed by an object plus an -ing form to say what someone was doing.
example: I saw him crossing the street.

name: You are
title: Verb "to be": you are
description: The pronoun 'you' combines with 'are', the second-person form of 'to be', used in simple statements about identity or qualities.
example: You are right about that.
note: Basic A1 'to be' form; appears at B1 only due to corpus sentence-position extraction, not a new teaching point.

name: few PLURAL NOUN
title: Few + plural noun
description: Few goes before a plural countable noun to mean 'not many, almost none', showing a small or limited number.
example: Few people came to the meeting.

name: little UNCOUNTABLE NOUN
title: Little + uncountable noun
description: Little goes before an uncountable noun to mean 'not much, almost none', showing a negative or limited amount.
example: We have little money left this month.

name: much UNCOUNTABLE NOUN
title: Much + uncountable noun
description: Much is used with uncountable nouns to talk about quantity, mainly in questions and negative sentences.
example: I don't have much time today.

name: so ADJ/ADV (that) CLAUSE
title: so + Adjective/Adverb (that) clause
description: 'So + adjective/adverb', optionally followed by 'that' and a clause, introduces the result caused by a high degree of a quality.
example: She was so tired that she fell asleep on the sofa.

name: too ADJ/ADV to+INFINITIVE
title: too + Adjective/Adverb + to-infinitive
description: 'Too' before an adjective or adverb, followed by a to-infinitive, shows that a high degree of a quality prevents an action.
example: It's too cold to go swimming today.
